title: Dependency injection

richText: Dependency injection is how Spring supplies one managed bean to another.
Spring supports constructor, setter, and field injection in Spring Boot applications.
also supports other injection methods, not only setters.
factory methods when it creates their returned beans.
For constructor injection, Spring resolves each constructor parameter before constructing the receiving bean.
It finds an eligible bean of the parameter’s type and passes that object to the constructor.
A component with one constructor does not need
The receiving class stores and uses the object with ordinary Java code.
can also identify the constructor to use when a class has several constructors.
The examples use constructor injection for required dependencies so those dependencies are present when construction finishes.

example.title: Supply the formatter to a service
description: The tabs contain one complete application for this injection type.
The project requires Java 17 or later and Maven.
explanation: Spring discovers `GreetingService` through `@Service`.
The constructor asks for a `GreetingFormatter` bean.
Spring supplies the registered formatter before the service is ready for use.
`greet("Ada")` returns `Hello, Ada` when a caller invokes it.
Startup creates the service. A caller must invoke `greet` to produce a greeting.

richText: For setter injection, Spring first constructs the receiving bean.
It then finds the dependency and calls the setter marked with
The setter stores the supplied bean in a field. The field is not supplied through the constructor.
A setter name alone does not request injection. In this annotation-based example,
requires a matching bean by default. A setter-injected dependency is not automatically optional.
allows Spring to skip the setter if its dependency is unavailable.
When the setter is skipped, the field keeps its initial value. The class needs a valid default or must handle the missing value.

example.title: Supply the formatter through a setter
description: The tabs contain one complete application for this injection type.
The project requires Java 17 or later and Maven.
explanation: Spring constructs `GreetingService` using its implicit no-argument constructor.
At the end of construction, `formatter` is still `null`.
Spring finds the `GreetingFormatter` bean and calls `setFormatter` before initialization callbacks run.
After injection, `greet("Ada")` returns `Hello, Ada` when a caller invokes it.
If no formatter bean is available, this required setter injection prevents bean creation.
Without Spring, a caller must call `setFormatter` before `greet`. The annotation does not make an ordinary Java call perform injection.

example.title: Supply the formatter directly to a field
description: The tabs contain one complete application for this injection type.
The project requires Java 17 or later and Maven.
explanation: Spring creates the service, resolves the formatter bean, and assigns it to the annotated field.
After injection, the service uses the formatter through ordinary Java method calls.
`new GreetingService()` does not ask Spring to inject the field.
Calling `greet` on that directly constructed object fails with `NullPointerException` because `formatter` is `null`.
The class declaration hides this dependency from its constructor. A plain Java caller cannot supply it through that constructor.

richText: Constructor injection makes required dependencies visible in the constructor and available when construction finishes.
It also allows those dependency fields to be
A plain Java test can construct the class and supply its dependencies without starting Spring.
Setter injection allows a dependency to be assigned after construction. It can support an optional dependency when the class has a valid default.
Field injection requires Spring or another reflective setup to populate the annotated field.
The course uses constructor injection for required dependencies. Setter and field injection remain supported alternatives.
Spring first looks for beans compatible with the requested dependency type.
No matching bean means a required dependency cannot be supplied.
A component outside the scan package or a missing bean definition can cause this failure.
Several matching beans require a selection rule for a dependency that expects one object.
Without a rule that identifies one candidate, bean creation fails rather than choosing an arbitrary object.

Other beans can then request the shared type without repeating a qualifier when that default is appropriate.
A primary bean must still match the requested type and any qualifier on the injection point.
Two primary beans among the remaining candidates do not identify a unique default.
narrows the type-matching candidates for a particular injection point.
A qualifier value can label a component class or a
The constructor parameter uses the same qualifier value to request that group of candidates.
For a single dependency, the remaining candidates must still resolve to one bean.
A bean name can also serve as a qualifier value when no separate label is declared.
A qualifier does not create a missing bean or make an incompatible type eligible.
An explicit qualifier can exclude the primary bean and select a different bean.

example.title: Choose a default greeting style and an explicit style
description: The tabs contain the three greeting-style classes, the application startup class, and the complete Maven build.
The project requires Java 17 or later and Maven.
Two beans have the same `GreetingStyle` type but return different greetings.
explanation: `@Bean` registers `casualStyle` and `formalStyle` as two beans of type `GreetingStyle`.
For the unqualified `defaultStyle` parameter, both beans match the type.
`@Primary` makes `casualStyle` the unique preferred candidate.
For `explicitStyle`, `@Qualifier("formal")` keeps only the bean carrying that label.
`casualStyle` is not eligible for that qualified parameter, even though it is primary.
Spring constructs `StyleDemo` with both selected objects.
A caller invoking `defaultGreeting("Ada")` receives `Hello, Ada`.
A caller invoking `formalGreeting("Ada")` receives `Good day, Ada`.
Startup wires these objects but does not call either greeting method.
Removing only `@Primary` makes the unqualified `defaultStyle` parameter ambiguous because neither bean name matches that parameter name.
That ambiguity prevents `StyleDemo` from being created and normally stops startup.
Changing only the parameter qualifier to `@Qualifier("missing")` leaves no matching bean and also prevents creation.

A constructor cycle exists when bean A requires bean B and bean B requires bean A.
Spring cannot finish creating either object in that cycle.
The application needs a different dependency direction or a separate component that coordinates the operation.
Changing field placement does not explain or remove the underlying cycle.
